meta.name: ISACA Certified Information Systems Auditor (CISA)
meta.notes: [initial release: 12 questions covering all five CISA domains — Information System Auditing Process (D1), Governance and Management of IT (D2), Information Systems Acquisition Development and Implementation (D3), Information Systems Operations and Business Resilience (D4), Protection of Information Assets (D5); balanced answer positions (3A/2B/4C/3D); ISACA auditor-lens phrasing throughout] | v1.1 (2026-07-03): +10 scenario questions across all five CISA domains — risk-based planning, evidence corroboration, SoD compensating controls, RPO/RTO strategy, data over-retention, access re-performance, self-review independence, batch run-to-run totals, SOC 2 reliance, change-exception expansion. Balanced correct positions. | [scheduled-agent hardening pass 2026-09-03: eliminated the consistent 'correct answer is longest' length tell that appeared in 19 of 22 questions by padding distractors to comparable length and trimming a few overlong correct options (notably cisa-015, cisa-017, cisa-021); upgraded obviously throwaway distractors (cisa-015 'faster hardware', cisa-017 'backups run slightly slower' / 'commended for indefinite retention', cisa-022 'shut down the change-management system', cisa-019 'project finished late') to plausible auditor-facing misconceptions; rebalanced correct-answer positions to A=6 B=5 C=5 D=6 with no adjacent runs of 3 (was A=6/B=5/C=4/D=5 with several longest-answer tells); rewrote every explanation so the reasoning cites BOTH why the correct answer holds AND why each distractor fails.]

questions.question: An IS auditor must conclude on the operating effectiveness of an access-review control across a full year. Which sampling approach provides the BEST statistical basis for projecting results to the population?
options: Judgmental selection biased toward the users the audit team already considers highest risk
Probability (random) sampling sized to a stated confidence level and precision target
Coverage limited to the review evidence for the first and last months of the audit year
Selection restricted to whichever review records the control owner chooses to hand over
questions.explanation: Only probability (random) sampling sized to a defined confidence and precision lets the auditor project the tested exception rate to the full population — the statistical basis required to conclude on operating effectiveness. Judgmental selection over-samples known-risk users and gives no basis to project across the rest, sampling only two months leaves the intervening ten months untested, and letting the control owner choose the records introduces selection bias and impairs auditor independence.

questions.question: An IS auditor must conclude on the integrity of a financial application's transaction log. Which evidence is the MOST reliable?
options: A signed letter from the application owner attesting that the log has not been altered
A screenshot captured by the lead developer showing the most recent transactions on-screen
A verbal walkthrough by the database administrator describing how the log is protected
Cryptographic hashes generated by an independent tool comparing two snapshots of the log
questions.explanation: ISACA ranks evidence by independence and objectivity, and cryptographic hashes generated by a tool outside the audited party's control sit at the top of that hierarchy. The owner's letter, the developer's screenshot and the DBA's walkthrough are all representations from interested parties and can be prepared selectively, so they carry materially lower reliability than the independent computational check.

questions.question: An IS audit manager with limited resources is drafting the annual audit plan and must decide which engagements to include from a large audit universe. Engagement selection should be based PRIMARILY on:
options: A current, documented IT risk assessment that ranks each auditable unit by exposure
The subject areas the auditee's leadership team has explicitly asked to have reviewed
The technologies the IS audit team is most familiar with and can therefore cover fastest
The scope covered in the prior-year plan, so year-over-year audit coverage stays continuous
questions.explanation: ISACA standards require the annual plan to be risk-based, prioritising engagements against a current documented IT risk assessment of the auditable universe. Auditee preference, prior-year continuity and auditor comfort each skew the plan away from the highest-risk areas: management input is one input to consider but cannot replace an independent assessment, and both prior-year rollover and covering only the familiar tend to leave the newest and highest-risk systems untested.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the newly formed IT steering committee's charter to assess whether the committee is positioned to align IT with business strategy. Which committee composition BEST supports IT governance objectives?
options: Only the CIO, the CTO and the head of infrastructure operations, chaired by the CIO
The CIO plus a rotating pool of project managers drawn from currently active initiatives
Senior business executives together with the CIO and CFO, chaired by a business leader
The CEO acting alone, taking IT investment decisions on behalf of the wider committee
questions.explanation: Effective IT governance requires the business to steer IT investment, so a committee that brings senior business executives together with the CIO and CFO — and is chaired by a business leader rather than the CIO — anchors decisions in business value and risk appetite. An IT-only membership biases the committee toward technology preferences, project managers operate at delivery level rather than portfolio governance, and CEO-only decisions bypass the deliberative peer review the committee is meant to provide.

questions.question: A small organization has too few staff to fully segregate database administration from application development, and management asks the auditor how to reduce the resulting risk. Which compensating control is MOST effective?
options: Requiring the DBA to take an uninterrupted block of mandatory annual leave every year
Independent review of DBA activity logs with alerting on privileged and sensitive actions
Rotating the combined DBA-and-developer role between two staff members every six months
Enforcing longer, more complex passwords on the shared DBA and developer administrator account
questions.explanation: When segregation of duties cannot be enforced, the strongest compensating control is a detective one: an independent reviewer monitors the privileged user's activity logs with alerting on sensitive actions, so misuse is spotted promptly by someone outside the role. Mandatory leave and role rotation only look back at a snapshot in time and miss anything done between cycles, and stronger passwords do nothing to constrain what an already-authorised privileged user can do.

questions.question: An IS auditor is engaged during the design phase of a new application. The auditor's PRIMARY role is to:
options: Assess whether the proposed controls adequately address the risks identified for the project
Take ownership of designing the application's internal controls jointly with the project team
Formally approve the final design so that construction work can proceed to the next phase
Author the test scripts that will be executed during user acceptance testing of the build
questions.explanation: ISACA stresses that auditor independence must be preserved throughout the SDLC: the auditor advises and assesses but cannot own control design, approve solutions or write acceptance tests, because each of those creates a self-review conflict at any later audit. The right role during design is to independently confirm that the proposed controls map to the documented risks the project is meant to mitigate.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviewing change management finds that emergency changes bypass the standard change advisory board (CAB) approval workflow. The BEST recommendation is to:
options: Eliminate the emergency-change path entirely so every change flows through the standard CAB workflow
Let the on-call engineer capture the change details in a ticket at their next convenient opportunity
Delegate emergency-change approval to whichever engineer happens to raise the incident ticket first
Fast-track emergency changes with formal CAB review and approval logged after implementation
questions.explanation: Emergency changes are a legitimate operational need; banning the path is unrealistic and pushes fixes underground. ISACA's expectation is a controlled fast-track: the change is applied to restore service and then formally reviewed and approved retrospectively by the CAB within a defined window. Unbounded documentation deadlines and self-approval by whoever raised the ticket both defeat the control by removing the independent oversight the CAB is meant to provide.

questions.question: An organisation has set an RPO of 1 hour and an RTO of 4 hours for its order-entry system. Which strategy MOST efficiently meets BOTH objectives?
options: Nightly full-database tape backups shipped to an offsite storage vault the following morning
Hourly transaction-log shipping paired with a warm standby server at a separate DR site
Weekly full backups held on a local NAS array kept inside the production data centre
Quarterly storage snapshots replicated to a second rack within the same production data centre
questions.explanation: A 1-hour RPO means data must be replicated at least hourly, and a 4-hour RTO means the recovery infrastructure must be pre-provisioned so it can be brought online well inside four hours. Hourly log shipping satisfies the RPO and a warm standby satisfies the RTO. Nightly tapes already blow the RPO by up to twenty-four hours, weekly backups blow it further, and same-data-centre snapshots offer no site diversity — a data-centre-level disaster takes both copies out.

questions.question: An auditor is evaluating whether an organization's backup strategy will actually work when a real disaster strikes rather than merely on paper. The MOST important indicator that the backup strategy will succeed during a real disaster is:
options: Documented evidence of periodic restore tests meeting the defined RPO and RTO objectives
The proportion of scheduled backup jobs that report a 'success' status on the console each night
The total capacity available in the offsite backup media library across all retention tiers
The cryptographic strength of the encryption algorithm applied to the backup media while at rest
questions.explanation: A 'success' status only confirms a job finished — organisations regularly discover at recovery time that the resulting backups were unreadable, partial or missing critical data. ISACA emphasises that only documented, successful restore tests against the stated RPO and RTO actually prove recoverability. Library capacity and encryption strength are useful operational concerns but say nothing about whether the data can actually be brought back.

questions.question: A corporate laptop containing customer records is stolen from an employee's car. Which control would have BEST limited the data exposure?
options: A strong BIOS password protecting the boot sequence of the stolen laptop from cold-boot access
A signed acceptable-use policy acknowledged by the user on the day they were originally hired
Full-disk encryption enforced with pre-boot authentication before the operating system loads
Antivirus software kept up to date with the latest signature definitions on the device itself
questions.explanation: Once a device is physically in an attacker's hands, only cryptographic protection of the data at rest meaningfully limits exposure: full-disk encryption enforced by pre-boot authentication keeps the disk contents unreadable without the key. A BIOS password is trivially bypassed by removing the drive and reading it in another machine, the acceptable-use policy is an administrative control with no protective effect against a thief, and antivirus addresses malware on a running system rather than physical loss of the device.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviewing user access in a financial system finds that 18 terminated employees retain active accounts up to 90 days after their departure. The BEST recommendation is to:
options: Run a quarterly access-certification campaign that covers every active user in the financial system
Require each line manager to email the IT helpdesk whenever a member of their team leaves the firm
Extend audit-log retention so missed departures can still be reconstructed by later reviewers
Integrate joiner-mover-leaver with HR so departures trigger automatic account deactivation
questions.explanation: The root cause is a process gap between HR and identity management. The strongest fix drives deactivation from the authoritative HR system, so terminations close access immediately and consistently. Quarterly certifications and manager-initiated emails are compensating detective controls that still leave gaps measured in weeks or months, and extending log retention has no preventive effect at all on how long the terminated access stays open.

questions.question: A financial reporting application is reachable from the public internet using only a username and password. Which control would MOST effectively reduce the risk of account compromise?
options: Requiring multi-factor authentication using a phishing-resistant factor such as a FIDO2 security key
Forcing every user to change their account password on a fixed 30-day rotation schedule
Restricting interactive logins to the organisation's local business hours in the head-office time zone
Raising the minimum password length to sixteen characters across every account in the system
questions.explanation: Credential phishing and password reuse defeat any password-only scheme regardless of length or rotation. Multi-factor authentication with a phishing-resistant factor (for example a FIDO2 security key) breaks the attack chain even when the password itself is known to the attacker. Frequent rotation actually weakens password quality in practice, business-hours restrictions are trivially circumvented by attackers operating from another time zone, and raw length still falls to a convincing phishing prompt.

questions.question: An IS auditor is planning the annual audit universe and must decide where to focus limited hours. Which approach is MOST appropriate for prioritising which systems to audit?
options: Audit whichever systems have been audited least recently, so coverage stays even across the audit universe
Audit whichever systems the CIO and other senior IT leaders nominate as most important to the business
Rank auditable areas by their risk to business objectives and allocate hours in proportion to that ranking
Rotate through every in-scope system alphabetically each year so no auditable system is ever skipped by chance
questions.explanation: A risk-based audit plan allocates scarce audit resources to the areas of greatest risk to the organisation's objectives — the professional standard for audit planning. Auditing by recency, by management nomination or alphabetically all ignore where the real exposure lies: management input is one factor but cannot replace an independent risk assessment, and even coverage is not the goal — proportionate coverage of risk is.

questions.question: During fieldwork an auditor discovers a control deficiency that management strongly disputes. What should the auditor do FIRST?
options: Escalate the disputed finding straight to the audit committee before discussing it further with management
Corroborate the deficiency with sufficient appropriate evidence and confirm it with management before finalising
Remove the disputed finding from the audit report to preserve the ongoing working relationship with management
Notify the external regulator that a compliance breach has been identified in the audited control environment
questions.explanation: An auditor must support every finding with sufficient, appropriate evidence and validate it with management before it is reported, giving management the chance to provide context or correct a misunderstanding. Deleting a supported finding compromises independence, jumping straight to the audit committee or a regulator skips the due-process the standards require, and premature external reporting is inappropriate before the finding is even substantiated.

questions.question: A company grants developers standing access to modify code directly in production 'for emergencies.' From a controls standpoint, what is the primary concern and the best compensating control if the access cannot be removed immediately?
options: The concern is degraded application performance; the compensating control is faster hardware for the environment
The concern is software licensing exposure; the compensating control is a periodic audit of installed software licences
The concern is a duplicated audit trail; the compensating control is deduplicating change entries in the ticketing system
The concern is a segregation-of-duties breach; the compensating control is independent review of logged production changes
questions.explanation: Developers with unrestricted production access breach segregation of duties — the same people who write code should not be able to move it into production unchecked, since that enables both error and fraud. When the access cannot be revoked at once, the standard compensating control is independent detective review: all production changes are logged and monitored, and an independent party reviews them. Performance, licensing and audit-trail deduplication each name a different concern and leave the SoD risk unmitigated.

questions.question: An organization's disaster-recovery plan specifies an RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 15 minutes for a core database. Which recovery strategy BEST meets both targets?
options: Asynchronous replication to a warm site combined with frequent transaction-log shipping to that same site
Nightly full backups of the database written to tape and shipped to an offsite storage facility each morning
Weekly full backups combined with a cold standby site provisioned from bare metal only when a disaster is declared
Manual re-keying of transactions from paper records preserved by branch staff after a prolonged outage
questions.explanation: An RPO of 15 minutes means at most 15 minutes of data loss and an RTO of 4 hours means recovery within 4 hours; a warm site fed by frequent log shipping and near-real-time replication meets both targets. Nightly or weekly backups leave hours to days of data loss (RPO fail), a cold site provisioned on demand almost never restores inside 4 hours (RTO fail), and manual re-keying satisfies neither and is inherently error-prone.

questions.question: An auditor reviews a firm's data-retention practices and finds emails are kept indefinitely 'just in case.' What is the main risk the auditor should raise?
options: Longer retention should be recommended as a security strength because more historical data improves anomaly detection
The only meaningful downside is that overnight backup jobs will run slightly slower against the larger email store
Over-retention raises storage cost, expands legal e-discovery exposure and can breach data-minimisation obligations
Retention length is purely an operational IT decision with no bearing on any legal or compliance requirement in force
questions.explanation: Keeping data longer than needed raises cost, expands the e-discovery surface in litigation and can violate data-minimisation and privacy regulations. The auditor should recommend a defined retention schedule aligned to legal and regulatory requirements, with defensible disposal. Indefinite retention is not an unqualified strength (the security value is dwarfed by exposure), the issue is far more than backup speed, and retention has clear legal and compliance implications well beyond IT.

questions.question: A CISA is assessing a newly deployed application's user access. Which test provides the STRONGEST evidence that access rights match policy?
options: Ask the application's system administrator whether user access is currently configured correctly against policy
Read the organisation's access-request policy end to end to check the document itself is complete and current
Confirm that a network firewall properly protects the application server hosting the newly deployed system
Independently re-perform a sample by comparing actual entitlements against approved requests and job roles
questions.explanation: Re-performance — independently comparing what the system actually grants against documented approvals and job roles — yields the strongest, most reliable audit evidence. Inquiry (asking the admin) is the weakest form of evidence, reviewing the policy tests design rather than operation, and a firewall check addresses network exposure rather than whether user entitlements actually match policy.

questions.question: An IS auditor participates in a project as an advisor during system development. At the post-implementation review, what is the primary threat to the auditor's objectivity?
options: The auditor may not yet have sufficient technical familiarity with the newly deployed system's internals to comment
The auditor could be reviewing controls they themselves recommended, creating a self-review independence impairment
The auditor is unlikely to be granted the level of access to production application and database logs the review needs
The project team may deliver the system after the originally agreed schedule for the go-live milestone had passed
questions.explanation: When an auditor advises on control design and later audits those same controls, they end up reviewing their own work — a self-review threat that impairs independence and objectivity. This must be disclosed and, ideally, the post-implementation review assigned to a different auditor. Technical familiarity and log access are project logistics rather than the core independence issue, and schedule slippage on the project itself, while relevant to project governance, does not by itself compromise the auditor's independence in the way self-review does.

questions.question: A batch interface transfers payment files between two systems nightly. Which control BEST ensures completeness and accuracy of the transfer?
options: Run-to-run control totals and record counts reconciled by the sending and receiving systems each cycle
A banner displayed at logon warning operators not to tamper with payment files while they are in transit
Encrypting the payment files at rest on the source system before the nightly transfer window even starts
Rescheduling the nightly job to run during business hours so operators can watch it complete on screen
questions.explanation: Run-to-run totals and record counts reconciled on both ends detect missing, duplicated or altered records — the core completeness-and-accuracy control for batch interfaces. A warning banner is not a control at all, encrypting only at rest addresses confidentiality rather than transfer completeness, and rescheduling so people can see it run does nothing to detect a data-integrity failure inside the pipeline itself.

questions.question: An organization outsources its data center to a cloud provider. What is the MOST important control the auditor should expect to see relied upon for the provider's control environment?
options: A verbal assurance from the provider's account executive that the environment is well controlled today
A marketing brochure supplied by the provider listing all of the certifications it has previously earned
The number of years the provider has been in business, treated as an indicator of control maturity
An independent assurance report on provider controls (e.g. SOC 2 Type II) with scope, period and exceptions reviewed
questions.explanation: When a third party operates key controls, an independent assurance report such as SOC 2 Type II lets the auditor rely on tested evidence of control operation over a period — after checking the report's scope, coverage period, noted exceptions and any complementary user-entity controls. Sales assurances, marketing brochures and how long the company has been in business are not audit evidence about control effectiveness.

questions.question: While testing change management, an auditor finds several production changes with no record of approval. What is the BEST next step?
options: Conclude the change-approval control is operating effectively because the affected changes appear to be working correctly today
Recommend that the change-management system be taken offline until every missing approval has been fully investigated and retro-filed
Expand the sample to judge whether the missing approvals are isolated or systemic and evaluate the impact before concluding
Set the unapproved changes aside because production has remained stable and no incident tickets have been reported so far
questions.explanation: Unapproved changes are control exceptions; the auditor should widen the sample to judge whether the failures are isolated or pervasive and assess the impact before forming a conclusion. Concluding the control works because output looks fine ignores the deviation, recommending the change system be taken offline exceeds the auditor's role and would harm operations, and ignoring exceptions abandons the professional skepticism the standards require.
